questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Which structure forms the protein coat that encloses a virus's genetic material?
questions.option_a: Capsid
questions.option_b: Envelope
questions.option_c: Ribosome
questions.option_d: Cell wall
questions.explanation: The capsid is the protein shell surrounding the viral genome. An envelope, when present, is an additional outer lipid layer; ribosomes and cell walls are not standard components of viruses.

distractor_rationales.B: An envelope is an optional outer membrane, not the protein coat around the genome.
distractor_rationales.C: Viruses do not contain ribosomes for independent protein synthesis.
distractor_rationales.D: A cell wall is not a standard viral structure.

questions.source: Original Apex draft aligned to PM&DC Uniform Curriculum MDCAT-2025; requires academic review.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: A virus uses an enzyme to make a DNA copy from its RNA genome after entering a host cell. Which enzyme carries out this step?
questions.option_a: DNA ligase
questions.option_b: RNA polymerase
questions.option_c: Restriction endonuclease
questions.option_d: Reverse transcriptase
questions.explanation: Reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA using an RNA template, a defining feature of retroviral replication. DNA ligase joins DNA fragments; RNA polymerase makes RNA; restriction enzymes cut DNA.

distractor_rationales.A: DNA ligase joins DNA fragments rather than copying RNA into DNA.
distractor_rationales.B: RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA from a DNA or RNA template, depending on the enzyme.
distractor_rationales.C: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at particular sequences.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Which everyday situation does NOT transmit HIV?
questions.option_a: Sharing a meal and eating utensils
questions.option_b: Receiving contaminated blood
questions.option_c: Sharing injection equipment contaminated with infected blood
questions.option_d: Transmission from an infected parent to a child during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding
questions.explanation: HIV is not transmitted through ordinary social contact, shared meals or utensils. Transmission requires specific exposure routes such as infected blood or certain body fluids.

distractor_rationales.C: Shared equipment contaminated with infected blood can transmit HIV.
distractor_rationales.D: Transmission can occur during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: What is the main effect of an enzyme on a chemical reaction?
questions.option_a: It changes the final equilibrium position
questions.option_b: It increases the amount of product permanently
questions.option_c: It lowers the activation energy needed for the reaction
questions.option_d: It is used up as a reactant
questions.explanation: Enzymes speed reactions by lowering activation energy and are not consumed overall. They do not change the reaction's equilibrium position or the net energy change.

distractor_rationales.A: A catalyst changes reaction rate, not the equilibrium position.
distractor_rationales.B: A catalyst changes how quickly equilibrium is reached, not the final equilibrium amount.
distractor_rationales.D: Enzymes can be reused after a reaction.

questions.source: Original Apex draft aligned to PM&DC Uniform Curriculum MDCAT-2025; requires academic review.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Why can an enzyme act on some substrates but not on many others?
questions.option_a: Its active site has chemical and shape features suited to particular substrates
questions.option_b: Every enzyme can bind every biological molecule
questions.option_c: The substrate permanently becomes part of the enzyme
questions.option_d: The enzyme changes its amino-acid sequence for each reaction
questions.explanation: Substrate recognition depends on complementary properties of the active site, including shape and chemical interactions. Binding is temporary and does not require the enzyme's sequence to change.

distractor_rationales.B: Enzymes are selective; they do not act on every molecule.
distractor_rationales.C: The substrate is converted to product and released; it does not become a permanent enzyme component.
distractor_rationales.D: The enzyme's amino-acid sequence is not rewritten for each reaction.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: A competitive inhibitor occupies an enzyme's active site. Which change can reduce its effect in a simple competitive-inhibition model?
questions.option_a: Reducing substrate concentration
questions.option_b: Increasing substrate concentration
questions.option_c: Removing all enzyme molecules
questions.option_d: Lowering the temperature to absolute zero
questions.explanation: More substrate can outcompete a reversible competitive inhibitor for active-site binding. This does not mean every inhibitor can be overcome this way; the model applies to competitive inhibition.

distractor_rationales.A: Less substrate makes competition for the active site less favourable to substrate binding.
distractor_rationales.C: Removing enzyme stops the catalysed reaction rather than reducing inhibitor competition.
distractor_rationales.D: Absolute zero is not a practical biological condition and would stop molecular motion.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: An enzyme works best near neutral pH. At a very acidic pH, its activity falls sharply. What is the best explanation?
questions.option_a: The substrate becomes an enzyme
questions.option_b: The enzyme gains extra active sites
questions.option_c: The reaction no longer needs activation energy
questions.option_d: Changes in ionization can alter bonds and the active-site shape
questions.explanation: Extreme pH can change ionization of amino-acid side chains and disrupt interactions that maintain the enzyme's structure, reducing substrate binding and catalysis.

distractor_rationales.A: The substrate does not turn into an enzyme.
distractor_rationales.B: Extreme pH does not create additional active sites.
distractor_rationales.C: All reactions still have an activation-energy barrier.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: The Miller–Urey experiment is commonly discussed in relation to chemical evolution. What did it demonstrate?
questions.option_a: That the first living cell was created in the apparatus
questions.option_b: That organic molecules can form from simpler substances under simulated early-Earth conditions
questions.option_c: That modern organisms arose by spontaneous generation
questions.option_d: That natural selection occurs in a single individual
questions.explanation: The experiment produced some organic molecules under simulated early-Earth conditions. It supported the possibility of prebiotic chemical synthesis; it did not create life or prove the complete origin-of-life pathway.

distractor_rationales.A: The experiment did not create a living cell.
distractor_rationales.C: Spontaneous generation is not what the experiment demonstrated.
distractor_rationales.D: Natural selection acts on populations across generations, not as a one-time change in an individual.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: A population contains heritable variation in beak shape. During a period when hard seeds are common, birds with deeper beaks leave more offspring. Over generations, deeper beaks become more common. Which process best explains this change?
questions.option_a: Individuals deliberately change their genes when needed
questions.option_b: All members acquire identical mutations at the same time
questions.option_c: Natural selection changes the frequency of inherited traits across generations
questions.option_d: Traits acquired during an individual's lifetime are automatically inherited
questions.explanation: Individuals with a heritable feature that improves reproductive success contribute more offspring, so the feature can become more common over generations.

distractor_rationales.A: Natural selection does not involve organisms intentionally rewriting their genes.
distractor_rationales.B: The scenario describes differential reproductive success, not a simultaneous identical mutation.
distractor_rationales.D: This is not the mechanism of Darwinian natural selection.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Which statement best represents Lamarck's historical explanation of evolutionary change?
questions.option_a: Natural selection acts on inherited variation
questions.option_b: Traits strengthened or diminished through use or disuse were proposed to be passed to offspring
questions.option_c: Evolution occurs only when an organism chooses to change
questions.option_d: All species remain unchanged over time
questions.explanation: Lamarck proposed that use and disuse could alter traits and that acquired changes could be inherited. This is a historical theory, distinct from modern evolutionary genetics.

distractor_rationales.A: This describes Darwinian natural selection more closely.
distractor_rationales.C: Lamarck's proposal was not that organisms consciously choose their evolution.
distractor_rationales.D: Lamarck proposed that species change.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: After an antibiotic is used in a bacterial population, resistant bacteria make up a larger fraction of the survivors. Which explanation is most consistent with natural selection?
questions.option_a: Some bacteria already had heritable resistance; those variants survived and reproduced more
questions.option_b: Every bacterium intentionally developed resistance because it needed it
questions.option_c: The antibiotic taught bacteria a new genetic code
questions.option_d: Resistance is caused only by bacteria becoming larger
questions.explanation: Heritable variants with resistance are more likely to survive exposure and reproduce, increasing the frequency of resistance in the population. The change is not purposeful.

distractor_rationales.B: Natural selection is not intentional adaptation by individuals.
distractor_rationales.C: An antibiotic does not teach bacteria a new genetic code.
distractor_rationales.D: Cell size alone does not explain inherited antibiotic resistance.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Which heart chamber has the thickest muscular wall in a healthy adult, and why?
questions.option_a: Right atrium, because it receives blood from the body
questions.option_b: Left atrium, because it pumps blood to the lungs
questions.option_c: Right ventricle, because it pumps blood through the aorta
questions.option_d: Left ventricle, because it pumps blood through the systemic circulation
questions.explanation: The left ventricle generates the pressure needed to send blood around the systemic circuit, so its muscular wall is the thickest.

distractor_rationales.A: The right atrium receives blood and does not generate systemic pumping pressure.
distractor_rationales.B: The left atrium passes blood to the left ventricle.
distractor_rationales.C: The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: What is the main function of the atrioventricular valves during ventricular contraction?
questions.option_a: To allow blood to flow back into the atria
questions.option_b: To prevent blood from flowing backward into the atria
questions.option_c: To send blood directly from the aorta into the ventricles
questions.option_d: To oxygenate blood inside the heart
questions.explanation: When the ventricles contract, the atrioventricular valves close to prevent backflow into the atria. The semilunar valves open to allow ejection into the great arteries.

distractor_rationales.A: The valves prevent this backflow.
distractor_rationales.C: The aorta carries blood away from the left ventricle.
distractor_rationales.D: Gas exchange occurs in the lungs, not inside the heart chambers.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes an artery?
questions.option_a: It carries blood away from the heart
questions.option_b: It always carries oxygen-rich blood
questions.option_c: It has valves along its entire length
questions.option_d: It carries blood toward the heart
questions.explanation: Arteries are defined by carrying blood away from the heart. Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood, so oxygen content is not the defining feature.

distractor_rationales.C: Valves are typical of many veins, not arteries along their entire length.
distractor_rationales.D: Blood moving toward the heart is carried by veins.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: What is one major function of the lymphatic system?
questions.option_a: Producing red blood cells in all adult tissues
questions.option_b: Returning excess tissue fluid to the bloodstream
questions.option_c: Pumping blood from the heart to the lungs
questions.option_d: Producing digestive enzymes in the stomach
questions.explanation: Lymphatic vessels collect excess interstitial fluid and return it to the circulation. Lymphatic organs also contribute to immune defence.

distractor_rationales.A: Red blood cells are produced mainly in red bone marrow in adults.
distractor_rationales.C: The heart pumps blood through the pulmonary circulation.
distractor_rationales.D: Digestive enzymes are produced by digestive organs and glands.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Which cells differentiate to become the main antibody-secreting cells in a humoral immune response?
questions.option_a: Red blood cells
questions.option_b: Platelets
questions.option_c: Neutrophils
questions.option_d: Plasma cells derived from activated B lymphocytes
questions.explanation: Activated B lymphocytes can differentiate into plasma cells, which secrete antibodies that bind specific antigens.

distractor_rationales.A: Red blood cells transport gases and do not secrete antibodies.
distractor_rationales.B: Platelets help with clotting and do not produce antibodies.
distractor_rationales.C: Neutrophils are phagocytic innate immune cells, not antibody-secreting cells.

questions.source: Original Apex draft aligned to PM&DC Uniform Curriculum MDCAT-2025; requires academic review.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Why can a secondary immune response to a previously encountered antigen be faster than the first response?
questions.option_a: Memory lymphocytes remain after the first response and can respond rapidly
questions.option_b: The antigen becomes a red blood cell
questions.option_c: The body stops recognizing the antigen
questions.option_d: All antibodies remain permanently at the same concentration
questions.explanation: Memory B and T lymphocytes can persist after the initial exposure and respond more rapidly when the same antigen is encountered again.

distractor_rationales.B: Antigens do not become red blood cells.
distractor_rationales.C: Immune memory supports recognition rather than stopping it.
distractor_rationales.D: Antibody concentrations can change; memory cells are central to the faster response.

questions.source: Original Apex draft aligned to PM&DC Uniform Curriculum MDCAT-2025; requires academic review.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Which immune cell type can directly destroy body cells infected by a virus as part of specific cellular immunity?
questions.option_a: Erythrocytes
questions.option_b: Platelets
questions.option_c: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes
questions.option_d: Mature red blood cells
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes recognize infected cells displaying relevant antigen fragments and can induce those cells to die, limiting infection spread.

distractor_rationales.A: Erythrocytes are red blood cells and do not perform this immune function.
distractor_rationales.B: Platelets are involved mainly in clotting.
distractor_rationales.D: Mature red blood cells do not carry out cellular immune responses.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Which feature of an alveolus most directly supports rapid diffusion of oxygen into the blood?
questions.option_a: A thick wall made of several tissue layers
questions.option_b: A thin moist surface closely associated with capillaries
questions.option_c: A surface with no blood supply
questions.option_d: A small surface area and low ventilation
questions.explanation: Thin moist alveolar walls and a dense capillary network create a short diffusion distance and maintain gas exchange.

distractor_rationales.A: Thick walls increase diffusion distance.
distractor_rationales.C: A blood supply is essential for transferring oxygen into circulation.
distractor_rationales.D: A large surface area and effective ventilation support gas exchange.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: During normal inspiration, what happens when the diaphragm contracts?
questions.option_a: The thoracic cavity becomes smaller and pressure rises
questions.option_b: The lungs actively push air out
questions.option_c: The diaphragm moves upward and relaxes
questions.option_d: Thoracic volume increases and pressure inside the lungs falls
questions.explanation: Diaphragm contraction flattens it and increases thoracic volume. The resulting pressure decrease allows air to flow into the lungs.

distractor_rationales.A: Thoracic volume increases, so pressure falls.
distractor_rationales.C: The diaphragm moves downward as it contracts.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Which change is associated with long-term exposure to tobacco smoke?
questions.option_a: Improved ciliary clearance in the airways
questions.option_b: Damage to airway cilia and reduced efficiency of normal airway cleaning
questions.option_c: A permanent increase in alveolar surface area
questions.option_d: Complete prevention of respiratory infection
questions.explanation: Tobacco smoke can damage airway cilia and impair the mechanisms that help remove mucus and trapped particles. This is a harmful effect, not a preparation strategy or a recommendation.

distractor_rationales.A: Smoke damages rather than improves ciliary function.
distractor_rationales.C: Smoke does not increase healthy alveolar surface area.
distractor_rationales.D: No exposure can guarantee complete prevention of respiratory infection.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Which sequence correctly traces the normal route of food through the digestive tract?
questions.option_a: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine
questions.option_b: Mouth → trachea → stomach → large intestine
questions.option_c: Stomach → mouth → small intestine → oesophagus
questions.option_d: Mouth → liver → pancreas → small intestine
questions.explanation: Food passes from the mouth through the oesophagus to the stomach, then through the small and large intestines. The liver and pancreas are accessory digestive organs, not sections of the food passage.

distractor_rationales.B: The trachea carries air, not food, to the respiratory system.
distractor_rationales.C: The sequence is reversed and places the oesophagus after the stomach.
distractor_rationales.D: Food does not pass through the liver or pancreas.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: What is the main digestive role of bile?
questions.option_a: It digests proteins into amino acids
questions.option_b: It breaks starch into maltose
questions.option_c: It emulsifies large fat droplets into smaller droplets
questions.option_d: It is a protease released by the pancreas
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify fats, increasing the surface area available to lipase. Bile is not itself a digestive enzyme.

distractor_rationales.A: Proteases digest proteins.
distractor_rationales.D: Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder; it is not a pancreatic protease.

questions.source: Original Apex draft aligned to PM&DC Uniform Curriculum MDCAT-2025; requires academic review.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Which substrate is acted on by pancreatic amylase?
questions.option_a: Proteins
questions.option_b: Triglycerides
questions.option_c: Nucleic acids
questions.option_d: Starch
questions.explanation: Pancreatic amylase hydrolyses starch into smaller carbohydrate products, including maltose and short oligosaccharides.

distractor_rationales.A: Proteases act on proteins.
distractor_rationales.C: Nucleases act on nucleic acids.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: How do intestinal villi improve absorption?
questions.option_a: They reduce the intestine's internal surface area
questions.option_b: They increase the surface area available for absorption
questions.option_c: They stop all movement of digested nutrients
questions.option_d: They convert every nutrient into glucose
questions.explanation: Villi and their microvilli greatly increase the surface area across which digested nutrients can be absorbed.

distractor_rationales.A: Villi increase, not reduce, surface area.
distractor_rationales.C: They support absorption rather than stopping nutrient movement.
distractor_rationales.D: Different nutrients are absorbed in different chemical forms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: A human gene is inserted into a suitable microorganism so the organism produces human insulin. Which biotechnology approach is being used?
questions.option_a: Selective breeding only
questions.option_b: Recombinant DNA technology
questions.option_c: Simple filtration
questions.option_d: Artificial pollination
questions.explanation: Recombinant DNA methods introduce a gene into a host organism so that the host can produce a useful protein such as insulin.

distractor_rationales.A: Selective breeding chooses organisms with desired inherited traits; it does not insert a human gene.
distractor_rationales.C: Filtration separates materials and does not create a gene product.
distractor_rationales.D: Pollination is a plant reproduction process.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: Why can a monoclonal antibody be useful in a diagnostic test?
questions.option_a: It binds many unrelated targets equally
questions.option_b: It destroys every cell in a sample
questions.option_c: It can bind a particular target molecule with high specificity
questions.option_d: It converts RNA directly into protein
questions.explanation: A monoclonal antibody population recognizes a particular antigenic target, allowing that target to be detected in a test.

distractor_rationales.A: Monoclonal antibodies are selected for specificity, not indiscriminate binding.
distractor_rationales.B: A diagnostic test detects a target; it does not aim to destroy every cell.
distractor_rationales.D: Translation converts RNA information into protein; antibodies do not perform this process.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question_text: What is the main purpose of including a suitable antigen in a vaccine?
questions.option_a: To train the immune system to recognize the target and develop immune memory
questions.option_b: To replace all white blood cells
questions.option_c: To guarantee that a person can never become infected
questions.option_d: To act as a digestive enzyme
questions.explanation: A vaccine presents an antigen or instructions for making an antigen so the immune system can develop a targeted response and memory. Protection is not an absolute guarantee.

distractor_rationales.B: Vaccines do not replace white blood cells.
distractor_rationales.C: Vaccines reduce risk and severity but do not guarantee absolute protection.
distractor_rationales.D: An antigen is not a digestive enzyme.
